response.title: Do I need a transfer switch to use a solar generator with my house, or can I just run extension cords?
response.answer:
No, you don't need a transfer switch if you're just using extension cords to power individual appliances. You only need a transfer switch (or another approved isolation device) if you want your solar generator to power your home's existing electrical circuits.

There are three common ways to use a solar generator with your house.

1. Extension cords — simplest and cheapest
Shop

Plug appliances directly into your solar generator, using appropriately rated extension cords when necessary.

No electrician required.

No changes to your home's wiring.

Ideal for refrigerators, routers, lamps, fans, and electronics.

Limited by the generator's output and the extension cord's rating.

Best for: Occasional outages when you only need a few essential appliances.

2. Transfer switch — power existing house circuits
Shop

A licensed electrician installs a transfer switch and generator inlet, allowing you to power selected circuits through your home's existing wiring.

Use your normal wall outlets and hardwired lighting.

Power multiple selected circuits without running extension cords.

Safely isolate your house from the utility grid.

Typically costs several hundred to over $1,500 installed, depending on the equipment and installation.

Best for: Regular outages or a more convenient backup-power setup.

3. Interlock kit — another option for some homes
Shop

A compatible, approved generator interlock kit can allow you to feed your home's electrical panel from a generator inlet while preventing the main utility breaker and generator breaker from being on simultaneously.

This can be less expensive than a transfer switch, but compatibility, local code requirements, and the solar generator's electrical design must be checked.

Important safety considerations

Never plug a solar generator into a regular wall outlet to power your house. This is called backfeeding and can create electrocution and fire hazards.

Also, some solar generators have floating-neutral outputs or other electrical configurations that affect whether they can safely connect to a transfer switch or interlock. Not every model supports home-panel integration.

For extension cords, use grounded, properly rated cords, avoid overloading them, and don't run them under rugs or through doors where they can be damaged.

My recommendation

If you only want to keep your refrigerator, internet, and a few lights running during an outage, extension cords are usually sufficient.

If you want to use your existing wall outlets, ceiling lights, furnace blower, or other hardwired equipment, consider a professionally installed transfer switch or approved interlock.

Two questions:

What solar generator do you have (EcoFlow Delta Pro, Anker SOLIX F3800, Bluetti AC200, etc.)?

Are you trying to power just a few appliances, or do you want to power your house through its existing outlets?

With those details, I can tell you whether a transfer switch is necessary and which setup makes the most sense.
